reasoning_traces.think:
CBR is constructed as a descriptive metric that evaluates team performance through a composite of win percentage, strength of schedule, and box-score efficiency without relying on possession-level data. It avoids the predictive biases inherent in BPI and KenPom by focusing on body-of-work rather than future game projections. The method assumes that past performance reflects true team quality, which is validated via comparison with actual committee selections. Its uniqueness lies in its lack of reliance on preseason assumptions (like NET) and absence of soft caps on point margins (unlike KenPom). The failure mode occurs when qualitative factors dominate selection, such as injuries or eye-tests, which CBR cannot capture. The logistic regression model used to derive CBR’s components ensures statistical consistency, though it may underperform in outlier cases. Dualities emerge between CBR and other metrics: BPI and KenPom emphasize prediction, while CBR emphasizes description. This distinction allows CBR to serve as a stable anchor in GSI’s Bayesian framework and as a deterministic feature in GSE’s state-space modeling.
